items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: How to Calculate Your Exact Age in Years, Months and Days
items.summary: Your age is more than the year you were born subtracted from this year. For school admissions, medical forms, retirement planning and birthday milestones, the exact figure matters: years, months and days, not just a rounded number. The good news is that the method is straightforward once you understand borrowing, and you can check the result in seconds with AgeCalculator. Begin with your date of birth and today's date. First work out complete years: if your birthday has already happened this year, your age in years is this year minus your birth year. If it has not happened yet, subtract one more year. Next, count complete months since your last birthday. Finally, count the days since the last monthly anniversary of your birth date. That gives a clear result such as 34 years, 5 months and 12 days, rather than a decimal that is hard to use on a form. Sometimes the day or month in today's date is smaller than the one in your birth date, so you need to borrow. If today's day is smaller than your birth day, borrow the days from the previous month: add the number of days in that month to today's day, then subtract your birth day, and reduce the month count by one. items.title: Converting PDF to Word in the browser, without a server (and why layout is the hard part)
items.summary: Most "PDF to Word" sites ask you to upload the PDF first. That means your contract, your invoice or your medical report sits on someone else's disk, and you are trusting a privacy policy you have not read. It does not have to work that way. A PDF is a file format, and the browser can parse it. This post is how the conversion actually works when you do it client-side — including the part nobody tells you: converting a PDF to Word means throwing the layout away on purpose. This is the thing that makes the problem interesting. In a Word document, text is structured: a paragraph contains runs, a run contains characters. In a PDF, there are no paragraphs. items.title: Why I Chose a Node.js Queue for 429 Rate-Limit Retry in AI Image Storage
items.summary: An AI image generation job is only half-finished when the bytes exist. In a fintech pipeline, a 429 rate limit or dropped connection can make an upload fail after the image was created, so retry backoff has to protect the durable hand-off. Short answer: keep generation and object storage upload as separate queue jobs, persist the generated bytes (or a durable temporary reference), and retry the upload with exponential backoff using an object key derived from the job ID. Object storage is the durable sink; the queue owns recovery. Infrai can fit when one REST API and one credential let that queue switch storage vendors without changing its application contract. The expensive term is usually regeneration, not the final PUT. If a worker throws away a 12 MB image after a storage 429, the next retry pays for generation again and extends the review queue. Saving the bytes first changes the failure unit from “make the image again” to “resume one upload.” That also makes retention an explicit product decision. items.title: What Changes With the A2UI 1.0 Release
items.summary: This article walks through what changed between A2UI 0.9 and A2UI 1.0, how generated UI works on 1.0, and why it is better, using one currency agent built on both versions. A Google ADK agent on Gemini looks up exchange rates and answers with A2UI cards and charts, rendered by a Next.js CopilotKit front end over AG-UI. https://github.com/xbill9/currency-claude-agui-a2ui1 On 0.9 the model wrote the UI as JSON, figures included. On 1.0 it writes one line and the server does the rest. A rate card for "Convert 100 USD to EUR" is 223 tokens of 0.9 JSON, 139 tokens of 1.0 Express, and 21 tokens as a 1.0 server-side macro call. A 90-day history chart is 1,060 tokens of 0.9 JSON and 21 as a macro call. Counted with the Gemini tokenizer, for the same components. A2UI is a protocol for agents that answer with UI. The agent sends a description of components (cards, text, buttons, charts) from a catalog the client implements, and the client renders them with its own native widgets. The agent never sends code, so the client decides what can run. Instead of a null reference crashing your program at runtime, the compiler forces you to handle the empty case. items.summary: Short answer: schedule a one-hour media cleanup follow-up as a delayed queue message, not as a cron entry, and place only an opaque asset reference in that message. Keep the media and its deletion authority with the specialist processor or storage service. That result has an evaluation constraint. A queue is acceptable only when its available region, retention behavior, and processor role fit the publisher's data map. If an opaque reference cannot cross that boundary, keep the schedule in the approved database and let one periodic cron sweep enqueue due work locally. Latency and cost matter, but they don't override the trust decision. The deceptively simple alternative is a Node.js setTimeout. It keeps the webhook request short, yet a process restart loses the timer. A cron entry per asset survives that process and still models the problem badly: one-off business state becomes a growing collection of schedules. A delayed message states the actual intent. items.summary: I read a lot on a Kindle, and a lot of what I want to read only exists as a PDF. Some are clean exports with real text. Many are scanned books: 400 photos of pages, 180 MB, slightly crooked. You can send a PDF straight to a Kindle, but the result is bad. A PDF has fixed pages, so on a 6" screen the text is tiny and you can't make it bigger. What you want is an EPUB, which reflows to fit the screen and lets you change the font and text size, like a book bought from the store. The usual recipe takes four tools: one for OCR, Calibre to convert, something to shrink the images, then email or Amazon's app to send. items.title: Your script's HTTPS calls don't show up in your debugging proxy. Here's why, per runtime.
items.summary: You start a debugging proxy, your browser and your iOS Simulator traffic show up fine, and then you run a Node script or a Python job and... nothing. Or you get UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE / CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED. On macOS the proxy sets the system proxy, and apps built on Apple's networking follow it. Most things you launch from a terminal don't. A request only shows up in a proxy when the program: sends it to the proxy, and trusts the proxy's certificate authority. Every runtime has its own switch for both. Examples below assume a proxy on 127.0.0.1:8080 that serves its CA as a PEM file. cat /etc/ssl/cert.pem ~/proxy-ca.pem > ~/proxy-bundle.pem This one bit me. curl --cacert and Python's REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE replace the trusted list. If you point them at the proxy CA alone, every host the proxy is only tunnelling (not decrypting) now fails verification, because those hosts present their real certificate. A bundle of the normal roots plus the proxy CA works for both. curl -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 --cacert ~/proxy-bundle.pem https://api.example.com/v1/me From the environment, curl reads https_proxy, but for plain HTTP it only reads lowercase http_proxy. items.title: What the Sentry SDK drops after a 429 quota response
items.summary: I'm building an error tracker, and I needed to know what an official Sentry SDK does when my ingest answers "you're over quota". I couldn't find anyone showing the wire, so I put a stub server in front of @sentry/node and logged every request it got. The failure is silent. A Sentry issue from 2025 says users "struggle with “why isn’t it working”" until someone sends them to the Stats & Usage page. Nothing throws. Events just stop showing up. Node v24.22.1, @sentry/node 11.11.0 (run-0-versions.txt), all local on 2026-11-09. The server is a 55-line stub I wrote, not Sentry. What Sentry's servers do comes from their public docs. After one 429 with X-Sentry-Rate-Limits: 60:error:organization:usage_exceeded, I captured 10 errors and only 3 hit the wire: 2 accepted, 1 rejected. The other 7 never left the process. No queue, no retry, and one warn-level debug line. The SDK backs off for exactly what the header says. With a 5s window it sent one probe every ~5s. A bare 429 with no headers blocked everything for 60s. The SDK does report the loss in a client_report, but the report said 7 when 8 were lost, because it skips the event that got the 429. items.title: Next.js prefetches got me rate-limited on my own site. Googlebot had been fetching them by the thousand
items.summary: This article was created with the help of AI. The numbers come from my own site's Search Console and server logs. On October 8 I opened my own news site, promtime.net, on my phone and got Cloudflare's error 1015 instead of a page. My own rate-limiting rule had blocked me, and all I had done was read posts on it. The cause was a Next.js feature that exists to make the site feel fast. Two days later Search Console showed me the same feature from Googlebot's side. Between August 10 and October 22 Googlebot made 25,943 requests to the site, and Search Console filed 16,284 of them under "Other file type": not pages, not images, not scripts. When a scrolls into view, the Next.js router prefetches the page behind it. It requests the same URL with an _rsc parameter and an RSC: 1 header and gets back the React Server Components payload instead of HTML, so the click that follows feels instant. Googlebot renders pages with JavaScript, and the prefetches fire for it as well. All 990 example URLs Search Console lists for "Other file type" end in ?_rsc=. items.title: Reduced motion in Framer Motion: what I learned adding it to 150+ files
items.summary: Most sites handle reduced motion with one CSS rule. beUI's site has it too: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; } } It's worth having, but on a Framer Motion site it isn't enough. Turn on "Reduce motion" with only this rule in place, and drawers still slide in, tabs still spring and counters still roll. That CSS only shortens CSS animations and transitions. Framer Motion works out each frame of a spring in JavaScript and writes the result to the element's style, so the media query never sees it. I build beUI, a library of animated React components, and more than 150 of its files now read the reduced motion setting. Here's what I learned doing that. null import { useReducedMotion } from "motion/react"; const reduce = useReducedMotion() ?? false; useReducedMotion() returns true when the setting is on. It returns null during server rendering, because the server can't know. The ?? false gives you a plain boolean, so you don't have to remember the third case everywhere. Reduced motion doesn't mean no animation. People turn the setting on because movement makes them dizzy or sick

items.title: React 19.3 View Transitions: The Suspense Patterns That Keep an App Fast
items.summary: TL;DR React 19.3 (9 September 2026) made stable, and Next.js 16.4 ships it. In the App Router every navigation is a Transition, so boundaries animate with no extra code. An unconfigured boundary animates on every trigger. Start from default="none" and opt into the triggers you want. Follow the Suspense rule: fallbacks appear instantly, the reveal animates, cached content never animates. update="auto" default="none" around does all three. A DOM node above a boundary, a boundary in a layout, or a shared pair without share all disable animations silently. Reduced motion and clicks during animations are your responsibility, not React's. Most of the View Transition bugs that ship in React apps over the next year will come from animating too much, not too little. React 19.3 made stable, Next.js 16.4 bundles it, and the default behaviour is generous: an unconfigured boundary cross-fades on every Transition that touches it. That is pleasant in a demo and tiring in a product. items.title: Build a Sales Report API in ASP.NET Core with PDF, XLSX and CSV
items.summary: Sooner or later, most business apps need the same two things: a report someone can print, send or archive, and a spreadsheet with the same numbers that someone else can sort and filter. If you build them in two separate code paths, they drift apart. A total gets rounded differently, a column goes missing, a month filter behaves slightly differently. In this tutorial you build a small ASP.NET Core minimal API that generates a monthly sales report on the server and returns it as PDF, XLSX or CSV from one report definition. The report groups orders by customer, prints a subtotal per customer and a grand total, takes the month from the query string, marks the PDF as PDF/A-3b with one extra line, and saves its layout to JSON so you can load it back later. The report engine is sgcReports .NET, a headless engine with bands, expressions, data sources, pagination and PDF, XLSX, CSV and PNG export. You'll use the free Community package from nuget.org. Every code block below was compiled and run against version 2026.10.0, and the numbers you see in the output were checked against the sample data. The .NET 8 SDK. items.summary: Construye un agente de desarrollo .NET, Parte 3: haz que te recuerde El lunes por la mañana le pregunté a mi agente de desarrollo qué había estado haciendo el viernes. Ejecutó git status, puso en pantalla el nombre de mi propia rama y me dijo: "I can't see Friday's history, only the current state." No podía ver el historial del viernes, solo el estado actual. Es una respuesta honesta, la de un compañero que lo olvida todo cada noche. Y no podía decir mucho más, porque todo lo demás que el agente sabía de mi repositorio se lo había escrito yo en el system prompt: tres proyectos, cuál importa, qué advertencia es ruido. Ese párrafo era memoria escrita a mano, en el único lugar que el agente no puede actualizar. Este post cambia las dos cosas por una memoria que escribe el propio agente con la herramienta de memoria de Claude, y mide lo que una demo no muestra: qué decide guardar, cuánto cuesta cargarlo cada mañana y qué pasa cuando un recuerdo deja de ser cierto. items.title: Make title and meta description required props. If a page can ship without them, it will.
items.summary: Here's a pattern I've seen in nearly every codebase I've audited. There's a component, or a generateMetadata function, or a layout that sets the . It has sensible fallbacks: if a page doesn't provide a title, use the site name. If there's no description, leave it empty. If there's no canonical URL, skip it. Those fallbacks feel helpful. They're actually how hundreds of pages end up titled "Acme Inc" with no description and no canonical, and nobody notices for months. My opinion: SEO metadata should be required by the type system, not suggested by documentation. If a page can compile without a title, eventually a page will ship without one. Developers mostly know pages need unique titles. Content teams mostly know descriptions matter. The bugs don't come from ignorance. They come from: A new page type copied from a template that relied on the layout's fallback title. A refactor that moved metadata into a parent layout, so every child inherited the same values. A CMS field that's optional, so half the entries leave it blank. A dynamic route where the data fetch failed and the page rendered with defaults. items.title: My Mac windows kept landing on the wrong Space after every monitor swap, so I wrote a small app for it
items.summary: I use a MacBook with one external monitor at a time, and I swap between a few monitors during the week. Every time I plug a monitor back in, macOS brings the windows back to that screen, but not to the Space they were on. Chrome ends up on desktop 3, Slack on desktop 1, and I spend the first few minutes dragging things around. I wanted something that remembers, for each monitor, which Space every window belongs to. I couldn't find a tool that did exactly that, so I wrote LayoutKeeper, a small menu bar app. What it does: Saves a window layout per external monitor, keyed by the monitor's EDID, including which Space each window is on. When that monitor is plugged back in, it moves windows back to their saved Space and position. Tells Chrome windows apart by profile, so work and personal windows go back to the right places. Adds brightness keys for external monitors. What it doesn't do yet: when you unplug and go back to the built-in screen only, it doesn't restore a separate layout for that. There is an open issue for it (#2) and it's the next thing I want to build. It's free and open source (GPL-3.0), with builds for Apple Silicon and Intel: https://github.com/tumingke0/LayoutKeeper

After a lot of trial and error configuring the UI and backend logic, I finally wrapped up VaultyPDF. Instead of building just a basic file converter, I packed 15+ everyday document utilities into a single dark-mode dashboard: Core file handling: Merging, splitting, compressing, and page cropping. Security & privacy: Permanent document redaction and on-chain e-signatures. Tracking: Decentralized user metadata and file state tracking handled directly through Motoko canisters (main.mo). Frontend: React with a clean, dark-mode SaaS dashboard layout. Backend: Motoko canisters running on ICP for serverless execution without traditional cloud databases. items.title: Scaling Frontend Development: Understanding Micro-Frontends Architecture
items.summary: What Are Micro-Frontends? Micro-frontends represent an architectural pattern where a large web application user interface (the visible part of a website users interact with) is broken down into smaller, semi-independent micro-applications. Instead of building one massive frontend codebase managed by every developer simultaneously, different parts of the screen are built and maintained by separate teams. These smaller pieces are then seamlessly stitched together inside the browser to deliver a single, unified user experience. Imagine walking into a large, modern food hall. To you, the customer, it feels like a single dining venue with shared seating, cohesive lighting, and one pleasant atmosphere. However, behind the scenes, the pizza counter, the sushi bar, and the coffee shop operate as completely independent businesses. Each stall hires its own chefs, manages its own kitchen tools, updates its own menu, and orders its own inventory without needing permission from the neighboring vendors. items.title: Building a Private Classifier with Apple's On-Device Model and NLContextualEmbedding
items.summary: Apple's on-device model is a small language model that ships with macOS and iOS. It runs offline, costs nothing per call, and never sends your data anywhere. The model has roughly 3 billion parameters. Its context window was about 4,096 tokens at launch, and that budget covers instructions, prompt and response together. Check the context size on your target OS version, because it can change between releases. A long document will not fit, so plan to chunk it. Speed. It runs on the Neural Engine and GPU, and generation is fast enough to feel interactive on Apple silicon. Time to first token is short, so short classification calls come back quickly. Throughput varies a lot with the chip and with the length of the output, so measure on your own hardware before quoting numbers. What it is good for: Classifying and tagging text. items.title: Tim Peters, Python User #2 and Prolific Contributor, Dies At 74
items.summary: Tim Peters, one of Python's earliest and most influential contributors, died on July 15 at age 74. Known as Python's second real user, Peters created the Zen of Python and Timsort sorting algorithm while contributing to numerous core components. He also served as a Python Software Foundation director from 2001 to 2014. Adafruit remembers Peters in a blog post: He's best known for the Zen of Python, PEP 20, still printed by typing import this. In 2002, he gave Python Timsort, the sorting algorithm he designed for lists, later adopted by Java and Android. He also polished the cyclic garbage collector and the pymalloc allocator, worked on the dict implementation, the float object, the math module and Karatsuba multiplication in longobject, and wrote the first version of doctest, plus difflib, pickletools and tabnanny. He was a director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014. Before Python, he wrote compilers at Cray Research and speech-to-text software at Dragon Systems. The thread is full of recollections from core developers about his patient, detailed answers on the mailing lists, signed with his trademark . items.summary: A practical field guide for iOS developers building VPN and Network Extension apps with NEPacketTunnelProvider. Hi everyone, I've spent a good amount of time building and maintaining iOS apps with a Network Extension layer, and I keep seeing the same debugging questions: "My tunnel is stuck on Connecting", "my breakpoint in startTunnel never hits", "the VPN just drops after a few minutes with no crash." Packet Tunnel Providers are hard to debug because they don't behave like a normal app. This post collects the setup, tools and habits that saved me the most time. I'd love to hear what has worked for you too. A packet tunnel runs as an app extension, which means: It's a separate process. Your host app and the extension have different lifecycles, and Xcode attaches to only one of them by default. The system controls its lifecycle. iOS launches and kills the extension, not you. It can be started, stopped or restarted without your app being in the foreground. It needs a real device. Packet tunnel providers don't run in the iOS Simulator, so every test cycle goes through hardware. It has tight resource limits. items.summary: Garmin has its own programming language, its own toolchain and its own app store, and most tutorials about it are either years old or stop at "hello world". We just shipped Clay Sniper for Garmin watches, a training app for clay shooters, and went from the first commit to a store submission in two days. Here is how it is built, and a practical walkthrough for building your own Connect IQ app. This is part 1 of a series. Part 2 will be about watch faces. Garmin apps are written in Monkey C with the free Connect IQ SDK. The easiest editor is VS Code with Garmin's official Monkey C extension. You test in the bundled simulator, sideload a .prg file to your own watch over USB, and publish a signed .iq package through Garmin's web portal. If you know Java, JavaScript or Swift, your first app will run in the simulator in an evening. items.title: StampName
items.summary: StampName (https://stampname.app) is a native Swift macOS utility (macOS 26 or later) that batch-renames invoice and receipt PDFs on-device, with no cloud uploads or LLM calls. It reads the native PDF text layer, or runs Apple's Vision text recognition on scanned paper receipts, and applies deterministic Swift extraction rules to turn the printed date, vendor, invoice or reference number, amount, currency, and expense category into a clean filename such as 2026-03-31_GitHub_INV-401928_21.00USD.pdf. Every extracted value is outlined in colour on the PDF preview, and uncertain fields pause in amber for one-click selection. Name collisions get a suffix like _(2) instead of overwriting anything. Every rename is logged to a local SQLite undo journal, and undo checks inode and hash before it restores a name. You can test bundled sample invoices in the app without a key at https://stampname.app/download, or claim one of the first 50 free Pro Lifetime licenses (0 USD checkout via Polar, no card needed) at https://stampname.app/free?utm_source=devto. Regular pricing is 39.99 USD for Lifetime or 19.99 USD for Yearly, for up to 3 Macs.

The likely culprit? Uninterruptible power supplies running routine battery checks. From the report: Every minute, some uninterruptible power supplies perform routine battery checks, creating small but measurable surges in electricity demand. And it's like clockwork. "Unintended synchronization can generate recurrent and potentially amplified oscillatory behavior in large-scale cyber-physical energy systems." To figure it out, Witthaut and his colleagues analyzed high-resolution electricity measurements from buildings at the Forschungszentrum Julich research campus in Germany. items.title: Preparing iOS Apps for iOS 27.2 and iOS 27.3: Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode & Compatibility Testing
items.summary: Discussion topic for Swift and iOS developer communities | November 2026 iOS 27.2 is now out, and the first developer beta of iOS 27.3 landed on November 3. On the surface, 27.2 is a user-facing release: it adds or refines features in six of Apple's own apps. The 27.3 beta is where things get more interesting for anyone who ships web content or hybrid apps, because Safari is gaining two features that change how pages are framed and rendered: Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode. Point releases rarely come with big API announcements, but they regularly shift the environment our apps run in. items.summary: New York has forced T-Mobile to remove a 50GB monthly data cap from its $15 low-income broadband plan after regulators found customers who exceeded the limit had their speeds cut by more than 97%, to just 650 Kbps. "Additionally, the [Office of the Attorney General (OAG)] found T-Mobile restricted [New York's Affordable Broadband Act (ABA)] plans to areas with 5G coverage, despite offering standard-rate 25 Mbps plans in 4G areas, and intentionally coded its website to hide affordable plans from search engines," reports RochestFirst. From the report: Under the terms of the settlement, T-Mobile must: - Eliminate data caps on its ABA plans and deliver guaranteed 25 Mbps download speeds. - Expand ABA plan availability to all geographic areas where it offers fixed-wireless home internet service. - Make its ABA webpage indexed and easily discoverable via standard web searches. In addition to changing its backup policy, Yandex Cloud announced the launch of a new availability zone, designated ru-central1-f. items.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
items.summary: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...

items.title: How do you actually self-host securely?
items.summary: I recognize that the title is rather vague, but I'm completely green when it comes to self-hosting, so I figured here would be a good place to ask for some pointers given the discussions I sometimes see happening in the comments. I tried researching first through DDG and Google, but (and I recognize this might be a skill issue) most things I found are either SEO slop or trying to sell/market some service. For some more context and to give a concrete example as to what I'm interested in, I got my hands on a Raspberry Pi which I'd like to use to start tinkering with self-hosting. My main goal would be to host my (static) website on it, potentially adding more things in the future. Some people I asked this question recommended solutions like Cloudflare Tunnels to make it secure, but using such a provider almost feels like it defeats the point of self-hosting, so I'm curious whether it's viable to do it using open source tooling, any gotchas one might encounter, and generally any thoughts you might have on the topic. (Also, feel free to suggest a tag other than devops, I figured security doesn't quite apply since it's a question and not a write-up/resource regarding security.)

items.title: Swarm (/swarm) (10 minute read)

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: SpaceX no longer needs NASA, and that's a problem for America's space agency (34 minute read)
items.summary: NASA is no longer an indispensable customer for SpaceX. SpaceX is now increasingly disinterested in the US government for most contracts outside of data services. The company is still fulfilling its existing contracts with the government, and at a lower cost and generally higher reliability, but it is no longer signing many large new contracts for spaceflight and services in the traditional launch and in-space flight domains. It sees the vast bulk of its future revenue coming from AI.

items.title: Meta Reportedly Built A Humanoid Robot Prototype That Can Do Household Chores (2 minute read)
items.summary: Meta's Max robot is designed to help out around people's homes. The prototype was built with the help of a Chinese robotics company in roughly three months. Powered by Nvidia's Jetson Thor chips, the robot weighs roughly 106 pounds and is about 1.5 meters tall, and has a display that can show facial expressions, a built-in speaker, and hands designed to pick up small objects. Meta is already working on a second prototype with updates to the design of the robot's torso and hands, as well as a projector and additional sensors to help it handle stairs better.
